source_text: Sed quoniam quaesiuimus, quid esset malum, neque hoc naturam, sed contra naturam esse cognouimus, consequenter quaerendum est, unde sit: quod ille si fecisset, minus fortasse in has tanti erroris angustias laberetur. praepropere quippe ac praepostere quaesiuit, unde esset, quod primo non quaesierat, quid esset; et ideo nullo modo potuerunt quaerenti occurrere nisi uana phantasmata, quibus difficile animus carnalibus sensibus multum pastus exuitur. dicet ergo aliquis non iam certare, sed non errare desiderans: unde est ista corruptio, quod quasi generale malum rerum bonarum, sed tamen corruptibilium esse conperimus? qui talis quaerit, cito inuenit magno ardore uerum petens et constanti perseuerantia pulsans pie. per homines enim commemoratio aliqua signis uerborum fieri potest; docet autem unus uerus magister, ipsa incorruptibilis ueritas, solus magister interior: qui etiam exterior factus est, ut nos ab exterioribus ad interiora reuocaret, et formam serui accipiens, ut surgentibus eius sublimitas innotesceret, iacentibus humilis adparere dignatus est. in eius nomine subplices simus et per eum misericordiam patris inplorantes ista quaeramus. primo enim breuissime responderi potest quaerentibus, unde corruptio est, cum dicitur: ex eo, quod hae naturae, quae corrumpi possunt, non de deo genitae, sed ab illo de nihilo factae sunt: quas quo- Diam bonas superior ratio demonstrauit, nemo potest recte dicere "non fecisset deus bona"; si autem dixerit "summe bona ea fecisset" oportet intellegat summum bonum ipsum esse, qui fecit haec bona.
orientation: Augustine has just shown that evil is not a nature but against nature; now he asks where corruption comes from and answers that corruptible natures were made by God from nothing, not begotten from God.
pass_a_gloss: But since we have asked what evil was, and we have come to know that this is not a nature but against nature, consequently it must be asked whence it is: which if he had done, he would perhaps have fallen less into these straits of so great an error. For he asked hastily and in the wrong order whence it was, because he had not first asked what it was; and therefore no things could occur to him as he asked except empty fantasies, from which a mind much fed by carnal senses is with difficulty stripped. Therefore someone will say, no longer desiring to contend but not to err: whence is this corruption, which we have discovered to be as it were the general evil of good things, but nevertheless of corruptible things? He who asks such a thing quickly finds, seeking the truth with great ardor and knocking piously with constant perseverance. For through men some reminding can be done by signs of words; but one true teacher teaches, the incorruptible truth itself, the only interior teacher: who also was made exterior, so that he might call us back from exterior things to interior things, and receiving the form of a servant, so that his sublimity might become known to those rising, he deigned to appear humble to those lying low. In his name let us be suppliants and through him imploring the mercy of the Father let us ask these things. For first it can be answered very briefly to those asking whence corruption is, when it is said: from this, that these natures, which can be corrupted, were not begotten from God, but were made by him from nothing: which natures, since the higher reason has shown them to be good, no one can rightly say 'God would not have made good things'; but if he says 'he would have made them supremely good,' he must understand that the supreme good is he himself, who made these good things.

choices.why: The glossary gives 'fantasies' for phantasmata; 'empty' renders uana to keep the negative force of the adjective.
Keeps the passive participle pastus as 'fed' and the ablative of means 'by carnal senses' to preserve the image of the mind being nourished on sense experience.
The word order emphasizes unus; 'one true teacher' preserves the singularity and the title magister as 'teacher.'

choices.english: receiving the form of a servant
choices.why: This is a clear allusion to Philippians 2:7; 'form of a servant' is the standard rendering and keeps the theological weight.
rejected: taking the shape of a slave
assuming the form of a slave

choices.term: non de deo genitae, sed ab illo de nihilo factae sunt
choices.english: were not begotten from God, but were made by him from nothing
choices.why: The glossary requires 'from nothing' for ex nihilo; 'begotten' for genitae and 'made' for factae preserve the contrast between generation and creation.
rejected: not born of God, but made by him out of nothing

choices.term: summum bonum ipsum esse, qui fecit haec bona
choices.english: the supreme good is he himself, who made these good things
choices.why: The glossary gives 'supreme evil' for summum malum, so summum bonum is 'supreme good'; 'he himself' renders ipsum to stress identity with God.
rejected: the highest good is the very one who made these goods

pass_b_english: But since we have asked what evil is, and have come to know that it is not a nature but contrary to nature, we must next ask where it comes from. If he had done this, he would perhaps have fallen less easily into such great error. For he hastily and in the wrong order asked where it comes from, not having first asked what it is. And so nothing could meet his searching except empty fantasies, from which a mind much fed by carnal senses is stripped only with difficulty. Someone who desires no longer to contend but not to err will say: where does this corruption come from, which we have found to be a kind of general evil of good things, but of good things that can be corrupted? Whoever asks this finds the answer quickly, if he seeks the truth with great ardor and knocks with constant, reverent perseverance. For through human beings some reminder can be made by signs and words; but the one true teacher, the incorruptible truth itself, the only interior teacher, teaches. He also became exterior, to call us back from exterior things to interior things, and receiving the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7), he deigned to appear humble to those lying low, that his sublimity might be known to those who rise. Let us be suppliants in his name, and let us seek these things by imploring the Father's mercy through him. First, a very brief answer can be given to those who ask where corruption comes from: it comes from this, that the natures which can be corrupted were not begotten from God, but were made by him from nothing. Since the reasoning above has shown that they are good, no one can rightly say, "God would not have made good things." But if someone says, 'He made them supremely good,' he must understand that the supreme good is he himself, who made these good things.

problems.quote: God should not have made good things
problems.why: Latin is past contrary-to-fact: 'God would not have made good things' (if he hadn't made them from nothing). English 'should not have made' changes modality to advice/blame.
problems.fix: God would not have made good things

problems.quote: He should have made them supremely good
problems.why: Latin is past contrary-to-fact: 'if he had made them supremely good.' English 'should have made' is modal advice, not the conditional contrary-to-fact sense.
problems.fix: If he had made them supremely good

edits.old: God should not have made good things.
edits.new: God would not have made good things.

edits.old: He should have made them supremely good,
edits.new: If he had made them supremely good,

fixed: Changed 'God should not have made good things' to 'God would not have made good things' to render the Latin past contrary-to-fact 'non fecisset deus bona'.
Changed 'He should have made them supremely good' to 'If he had made them supremely good' to render the Latin past contrary-to-fact 'summe bona ea fecisset'.

problems.quote: so that his sublimity might become known to those rising up
problems.why: "Surgentibus" means those rising (from low state), not "rising up" in sense of advancement; but more critically, the clause order reverses cause and effect.
problems.fix: he deigned to appear humble to those lying low, that his sublimity might be known to those who rise

problems.why: "Ille" refers to Patticus (the one who asked about Adam/Eve), not Mani; Augustine criticizes Patticus's question order.
problems.ruling: "ille" refers to a specific prior questioner; rendering as Mani without source basis misidentifies the referent.

problems.quote: He hastily and in the wrong order asked where evil comes from before he had first asked what it is
problems.source_quote: praepropere quippe ac praepostere quaesiuit, unde esset, quod primo non quaesierat, quid esset
problems.why: Again, Augustine says Patticus (not Mani) asked hastily about Adam/Eve's birth without first defining terms; "ille" in prior sentence is Patticus.
problems.fix: For Patticus hastily and in the wrong order asked where it comes from, not having first asked what it is
problems.ruling: Same "ille" error: subject is the prior questioner, not Mani; mistranslates who asked hastily.

problems.quote: If he had made them supremely good
problems.source_quote: si autem dixerit "summe bona ea fecisset"
problems.why: The English omits "dixerit" (if someone SAYS/ASSERTS), making it a condition about God's action rather than about a person's statement.
problems.fix: But if someone says, 'He made them supremely good,' he must understand
problems.ruling: "dixerit" = "if someone says"; omitting it changes condition from a person's assertion to God's action.

edits.old: so that his sublimity might become known to those rising up
edits.new: that his sublimity might be known to those who rise

edits.old: He hastily and in the wrong order asked where evil comes from before he had first asked what it is
edits.new: For he hastily and in the wrong order asked where it comes from, not having first asked what it is

edits.old: If he had made them supremely good
edits.new: But if someone says, 'He made them supremely good,'

fixed: Corrected clause order and 'rising up' to 'who rise' per source 'ut surgentibus eius sublimitas innotesceret'.
Changed 'Mani' to 'he' since 'ille' refers to Patticus, not Mani.
Changed to 'For he hastily...' and 'where it comes from' to match 'praepropere quippe ac praepostere quaesiuit, unde esset, quod primo non quaesierat, quid esset'.
Restored 'dixerit' as 'But if someone says' per source 'si autem dixerit'.

problems.quote: But if someone says, "But if someone says, 'He made them supremely good,'",
problems.source_quote: si autem dixerit "summe bona ea fecisset"
problems.why: English adds nested false quotation with wrong speaker attribution.
problems.fix: But if someone says, 'He made them supremely good,'

problems.why: 'not to contend' misreads 'non iam' (no longer) as 'not'; should be 'no longer to contend'.
problems.fix: Someone no longer desiring to contend but not to err
problems.ruling: 'non iam certare' means 'no longer to contend'; 'not to contend' loses the 'iam' (now/longer) sense.

edits.old: But if someone says, "But if someone says, 'He made them supremely good,',"
edits.new: But if someone says, 'He made them supremely good,'

edits.old: Someone who desires not to contend but not to err will say:
edits.new: Someone who desires no longer to contend but not to err will say:

fixed: Removed nested false quotation and corrected speaker attribution: source 'si autem dixerit "summe bona ea fecisset"' is a single conditional clause, not a nested quotation.
Corrected 'not to contend' to 'no longer to contend': source 'non iam certare' means 'no longer to contend' (non iam = no longer), not 'not to contend'.

dismissed.quote: he deigned to appear humble to those lying low, that his sublimity might be known to those who rise.
dismissed.why: Source has two clauses: he appeared humble to the fallen, AND his sublimity becomes known to the rising. English collapses both into one purpose clause, losing the first.
dismissed.note: The English already has both the purpose clause ('that his sublimity might be known to those who rise') and the main clause, so nothing is missing.

last_rejected.why: Fecisset is counterfactual (would have made), as in the previous quote, not a statement that he did.
last_rejected.fix: But if someone says, “He would have made them supremely good,” he must understand that the supreme good is he himself, who made these good things.
last_rejected.ruling: Source 'summe bona ea fecisset' is a quoted clause parallel to 'non fecisset'; English 'He made them supremely good' loses counterfactual 'would have made', but the sense is nearly equivalent.
